organization.name: Civic Order Mail Service
organization.entry:
Official Name: The Civic Order Office of Posts, Parcels, Notices & Lawful Correspondence
Common Names: Civic Post, the Mail Service, the Bluecoats
Employees: Post Carriers, Sorters, Letter Clerks, Dead-Mail Examiners, Parcel Inspectors, Route Surveyors
Motto: ‘Neither Fog Nor Flood Shall Prevent Lawful Delivery.’

The Civic Order Mail Service is Fogport's official postal system, responsible for carrying letters, parcels, government notices, summonses, newspapers, bills, death announcements, warrants, invitations, and other properly addressed matter throughout the city.

It is also one of the few branches of the Civic Order that ordinary Fogporters grudgingly admit works rather well.

A letter posted in the Shambles will probably reach Blackwake.

Eventually.

Possibly damp.

And perhaps bearing several stamps explaining why it was opened.

But it will probably arrive.

Post Carriers are immediately recognizable by their dark blue uniforms, striped black-and-brass cuffs, heavy satchels, and the Civic Postal Standard they carry on their routes.

Everyone else calls it a Mailstick.

The Mailstick

The Mailstick is both equipment and badge of office.

It is a tall iron-and-brass staff fitted with a small locked posting box, route pennant, identification plate, and sometimes a hooded oil lamp for night deliveries. A carrier plants the Standard at street corners while making deliveries nearby, allowing citizens to deposit outgoing letters directly into it.

The staff also establishes a small but legally significant piece of temporary Civic territory around itself.

Under an obscure postal ordinance, an on-duty carrier standing within six feet of a planted Postal Standard has right-of-way and limited Civic authority.

This includes the right to:

  • cross certain barricades and checkpoints;
  • demand passage through obstructed streets;
  • enter common stairwells and courtyards;
  • ride Civic trams without fare;
  • demand directions to a registered address;
  • request assistance from Civic Vigilance officers;
  • and shout ‘MAKE WAY FOR THE POST’ with legal force.

Impersonating a postal carrier is consequently a serious crime.

Stealing a Mailstick is considerably worse.

Nobody is entirely certain why.

The Grand Sorting House

The headquarters of the Mail Service is the enormous Grand Sorting House of Fogport, usually called simply the Sort.

It occupies a soot-blackened former railway terminus near Heliot Station, where several abandoned rail lines once converged.

Its great arched facade bears the inscription:

EVERY PERSON HAS AN ADDRESS.

Inside, hundreds of clerks work beneath an immense iron-and-glass roof.

Letters travel through the building in canvas sacks, brass pneumatic tubes, overhead wire baskets, gravity chutes, handcarts, miniature rail wagons, and an antiquated system of continuously moving chains from which bundles of correspondence hang like drying fish.

The noise is tremendous.

Bells indicate incoming routes.

Whistles indicate outgoing routes.

A gong indicates government correspondence.

Three gongs indicate a parcel that has begun moving by itself.

Employees are instructed not to investigate until the Dead-Mail Office arrives.

Beneath the main floor lies an older complex of tunnels, storage vaults and forgotten sorting chambers dating back through several previous governments.

Some are still in use.

Others appear on no current plans.

Mail occasionally comes out of them.

The Dead-Mail Office

Undeliverable correspondence is never thrown away.

This is Civic policy.

If an address cannot be found, the recipient is dead, the building has disappeared, the street no longer exists, or the intended recipient apparently never existed in the first place, the item is transferred to the Office of Dead Correspondence.

Dead-Mail Clerks attempt to determine where the letter ought to have gone.

This can take years.

The office contains shelves upon shelves of unresolved correspondence.

Some letters are centuries old.

Some are addressed to kings who died before Fogport had its present name.

Some are addressed to people who have not yet been born.

There is an entire locked cabinet labeled:

LETTERS ADDRESSED TO FOGPORT ITSELF

Nobody admits to having the key.

Postal Law

Fogport's postal statutes are ancient, contradictory and treated with startling seriousness.

Opening another person's properly sealed mail without authorization is a Civic offense.

Destroying registered mail is worse.

Knowingly obstructing a carrier can result in a fine.

Robbing one can result in imprisonment.

Deliberately killing a uniformed carrier while they are in possession of registered Civic correspondence technically constitutes Interference With Delivery of the First Degree.

The punishment prescribed in the original statute is:

‘Completion of Delivery by Whatever Means Necessary, followed by Hanging.’

The Mail Service still occasionally invokes it.

This has given rise to a traditional Fogport warning:

‘Never kill the postman until you've checked his bag.’

The Routes

Every carrier possesses an assigned Route Book containing addresses, shortcuts, service tunnels, roof crossings, tram schedules, building entrances and handwritten warnings accumulated by previous carriers.

These books are extremely valuable.

Some contain routes through Fogport that appear on no ordinary map.

There are stairs accessible only through kitchens.

Bridges connecting rooftops.

Doors through warehouses whose owners have been legally required to permit postal passage for generations.

One famous postal route allegedly passes straight through a private bedroom because the Civic Order established the route eighty-seven years before the house was built around it.

The resident is required to leave the bedroom door unlocked between 10:15 and 10:22 every morning except Civic holidays.

Postal Weirdness

Carriers are notoriously superstitious.

Never whistle while sorting international post.

Never deliver a black envelope after sunset.

If a letter has no return address, knock only twice.

If the recipient says, ‘I wasn't expecting anything,’ the carrier must answer:

‘Expectation is not required for delivery.’

If a house has vanished, do not mark the letter undeliverable until you have checked the address again tomorrow.

And carriers absolutely refuse to discuss Route Zero.

According to official records, there is no Route Zero.

Nevertheless, every few months somebody at the Sort finds a canvas mailbag bearing a large brass 0 hanging among the incoming sacks.

It is always full.

Adventure Hooks

The Impossible Address

Byl and Lott acquire a letter addressed to someone they desperately need to find. The address isn't on any map—but an elderly carrier recognizes it immediately.

‘Oh. That's Old Route Seventeen.’

Unfortunately, nobody has walked Old Seventeen since three carriers disappeared there twenty-two years ago.

The Missing Mailman

A carrier disappears halfway through his route. Civic Vigilance assumes robbery.

The Mail Service doesn't particularly care about the carrier—they desperately want back one particular registered parcel in his bag.

Mercy knows somebody willing to pay considerably more for it.

Route Zero

Byl notices a postal carrier walking through Nine Spoons at three in the morning.

Wrong uniform.

Old-fashioned Mailstick.

Nobody else seems particularly interested.

The carrier leaves a letter addressed simply:

BYL HASBAINE — DELIVER PERSONALLY.

The Great Postal Robbery

Somebody learns that the Civic Treasury routinely moves bearer bonds and payroll certificates through ordinary registered mail because nobody is stupid enough to rob the post.

Naturally, somebody becomes stupid enough.

The Dead Letter

A forty-year-old letter turns up addressed to someone Byl knows.

It describes something that supposedly happened during the Catastrophe—but contradicts the accepted story in one extremely important detail.

Special Delivery

A mortally wounded carrier presses his Mailstick into Byl's hands and invokes an obscure provision of Civic law making him an Emergency Auxiliary Post Carrier until the registered item in the satchel reaches its destination.

Byl suddenly possesses remarkable legal privileges.

He also inherits the people trying to stop the delivery.

And somewhere in the Grand Sorting House, a clerk stamps a card:

HASBAINE, BYL — TEMPORARY POSTAL EMPLOYEE.

Which may prove considerably harder to undo than expected.
